core.text: For wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do, a verb takes the shape of **the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come)**. The forms change one vowel: first conjugation swaps its -ā- for -ē- (*laudat → laudet*); the others put -ā- before the ending (*videat, pōnat, audiat*). Endings are the ordinary -m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt, active or passive. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus praesentis*.
English lost most of its subjunctive; its shadow survives in *God save the king* and *so be it*.
1st conjugation: -em, -ēs, -et, -ēmus, -ētis, -ent. 2nd, 3rd, 4th: -am, -ās, -at, -āmus, -ātis, -ant. Irregular: sim, possim, velim, nōlim, mālim (with -i-); eam, feram, fīam.

invented.la: Magister discipulōs monet ut taceant et audiant.
invented.en: The teacher warns the pupils to be quiet and listen.

core.text: In the third and fourth conjugations **the future (the 'will do' tense)** has -ē- (*scrībet* — he will write) where the subjunctive has -ā- (*scrībat* — let him write). In the first conjugation it is -bit against -et: *laudābit* / *laudet*. Only *scrībam* is shared; the sentence decides.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) treat -a- as the subjunctive marker, contracting with an ā-stem into -e- (*ambulem*), and give the irregulars: *sim, sīs, sit*; *possim*; *eam, eās, eat*; *velim*; *nōlim*; *mālim*. Passive endings follow the same vowel: *laudētur, videātur, pōnātur, audiātur*.

Ørberg (cap. XXVII) introduces the mood through commands reported with *ut*: *dominus servō imperat ut intret, forem claudat, taceat et audiat*. Where the forms go — wishes, orders, purpose, indirect questions — is the business of the next lessons; this one is about recognising the vowel.

teach.title: What the form is for
teach.say: For a wish, a purpose, or what one person tells another to do, the verb changes shape into **the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come)**. *Dominus servō imperat ut intret* — the master orders the slave to come in. *Ut* ('that') usually stands in front of it, or *nē* for 'that … not'.

teach.title: First conjugation: -a- becomes -e-
teach.say: A first-conjugation verb swaps its *-a-* for *-e-*: *portat → portet*, *clāmat → clāmet*, *nārrat → nārret*. Everything after that vowel is the ordinary set of person endings, *-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*.

show.say: portet — the -a- of portat has turned into -e-

teach.title: Every other conjugation: slide an -a- in
teach.say: The second, third and fourth conjugations put an *-a-* in before the ending instead: *tacet → taceat*, *claudit → claudat*, *audit → audiat*, *lūdunt → lūdant*. The *-iō* verbs of the third keep their *i*: *facit → faciat*, *capit → capiat*. One vowel is the entire change, in both numbers and all three persons.

show.say: taceat — the -a- slides in in front of the ending

teach.title: The verbs that go their own way
teach.say: *Sum* and its relatives take an *-i-* instead: *sit*, *possit*, *velit*, *nōlit*. *Eō* has *eat*, *ferō* has *ferat*, *fīō* has *fīat*. *Pater imperat ut fīlius Rōmam eat* — the father orders his son to go to Rome.

show.say: sit — sum takes -i- where the others take -e- or -a-

teach.title: Telling it from the future
teach.say: In the third and fourth conjugations the future carries *-e-* exactly where the subjunctive carries *-a-*: *scrībet*, he will write; *scrībat*, that he write. In the first conjugation the two are further apart — *labōrābit* against *labōret* — because the future there has *-bit*. Only the 'I' form is shared: *scrībam* is both 'I shall write' and 'that I write', and the sentence decides.

teach.title: Using it with no ut at all
teach.say: The same form stands alone for a wish or for an order given about someone else: *Veniat Mārcus!*, let Marcus come; *Deī nōs iuvent!*, may the gods help us. The passive keeps the same vowel and adds the passive endings: *claudātur*, that it be shut.
